source_read: PMC HTML, PMC8097729 (full text read in own browser tab: abstract, introduction, methods, results incl. Tables 1-5, figure captions, discussion, declarations). Figures 1-3 not read as images (their captions were read); Supplementary Table S1 (full GSEM results) not read.

claims.overstatement: None; the claim says 'associated' and 'small amounts', where the authors speak of a network of causal relationships (Methods) and of setting and set that appear to have significant effects (conclusion). One wording point: 'fasting ... was associated with no difference' would be safer as 'no detectable difference' (fear -0.07, 95% CI -0.29 to 0.15 on 0-10; Kessler-10 -0.28, -0.69 to 0.13; editors' intervals from the printed SEs).
claims.note: Every Perkins number in statement and magnitude checked against Table 2-5 and the Results: 3,553 + 1,338 + 1,926 = 6,817 (52.1%, 19.6%, 28.3%; 60 without a known setting); church members 87.0% living in Brazil, 28.3% + 28.5% = 56.8% over 200 uses; five uses or fewer 68.0% (other) and 66.0% (traditional); support-and-safety means 3.4 to 3.9; fear CI -0.43 to -0.15; whole-range Kessler differences 1.86 (support) and 0.75 (preparation) points. Three qualifications: (1) the paper says linear regression was used for continuous and stereotype logistic regression for ordinal outcomes without saying which outcomes were which, so reading B = -0.29 as points on the 0-10 fear item assumes a linear model (plausible, not stated); the paper also gives no mean or SD for the fear item or the difficulty count, so the coefficients cannot be set against their spread; (2) ceremony features and ratings refer to the last context of consumption, while the fear item asks about 'the ayahuasca session' without saying which one (many church members had hundreds); (3) the models also included the three motivation scores and all other ceremony and support variables, not only the listed covariates (the claim's later sentence on therapeutic reasons reflects this). Missing data were multiply imputed (m = 20), so every model reports n = 6,877.

anchors.locator: Materials and Methods > Study Design (1st paragraph)
anchors.extracted: Cross-sectional online survey 2017-2019 in English plus five other languages; adults who had drunk ayahuasca at least once; non-random sampling via organisations, retreat centres, churches, online groups, Facebook and flyers; no incentives; 10,836 respondents in more than 50 countries, of whom those who had drunk with two or fewer groups (n = 6,877) were analysed; partial completions retained.

anchors.locator: Results (1st paragraph); Table 3, rows 'All respondents', 'Region of residence', 'Number of times drunk', 'Time since last drank'
anchors.extracted: Last context: ayahuasca church 52.1% (n = 3,553), traditional 19.6% (1,338), other 28.3% (1,926); total 6,817. Church: 87.0% living in Brazil; 201-500 uses 28.3% and 500-5000 uses 28.5%. Five uses or fewer: traditional 18.6 + 27.0 + 20.4 = 66.0%, other 19.8 + 30.4 + 17.8 = 68.0%. Years since last drank, mean (SD): 1.2 (4.7), 1.6 (3.1), 1.2 (2.5).

anchors.locator: Materials and Methods > Demographic and Ayahuasca Drinking Variables (2nd paragraph); Table 1; Statistical Analysis (4th paragraph)
anchors.extracted: Ceremony characteristics ticked for the last context of consumption; six support, safety and preparation items rated 1 (not at all) to 4 (very much). Factor analysis gave a traditional count (0-6), a non-traditional count (0-5), a support-and-safety mean (four items, means 3.7-3.8) and a preparation mean (two items: opportunity to discuss history, motivations or concerns before drinking, and guidance before drinking about potential difficulties; means 3.1).

anchors.locator: Materials and Methods > Demographic and Ayahuasca Drinking Variables (3rd paragraph); Mental Health, Wellbeing and Spirituality Variables (1st and 3rd paragraphs)
anchors.extracted: Extreme fear or panic: one item, 0 (not at all) to 10 (very much), 'during the ayahuasca session' (which session is not stated). Integration difficulties: count from PHQ-4 plus five items for the weeks or months after drinking. Kessler-10 range 10-50 (higher = more distress). SIMO: nine items, total 9-90.

anchors.locator: Materials and Methods > Statistical Analysis (1st and 2nd paragraphs)
anchors.extracted: Linear regression for continuous and stereotype logistic regression for ordinal outcomes (outcome-by-outcome model type not given); multicollinearity screened (VIF > 3, correlations > 0.7); missing data multiply imputed by chained equations, m = 20.

Adjusted B (SE), n = 6,877: support and safety -0.29 (0.07), p < 0.001; preparation -0.01 (0.04), p = 0.816; traditional practices 0.18 (0.03); traditional countries 0.7 (0.14); therapeutic motivation 0.21 (0.03); lifetime mental-health diagnoses 0.21 (0.04); religious (hymns or sermons) -0.38 (0.09); age per decade -0.22 (0.03); also non-traditional 0.1 (0.04), p = 0.007, religious or spiritual counselling -0.26 (0.09), p = 0.004, university education 0.15 (0.08), p = 0.041; fasting -0.07 (0.11), p = 0.566. Same model holds age, sex, education, diagnoses, times drunk, years since drinking, three motivation scores, ceremony and support variables.

Support and safety -0.13 (0.05), p = 0.018; preparation -0.14 (0.03), p < 0.001; fasting -0.05 (0.08), p = 0.545; religious -0.15 (0.07), p = 0.028; therapeutic motivation 0.15 (0.02); non-traditional 0.09 (0.03).

anchors.locator: Table 2, row 'Fasting (y/n)' and 'Safe and supported score'; Table 4, column 'SIMO score', row 'Fasting'; Table 5, row 'Fasting'
anchors.extracted: Fasting offered: church 2.0%, traditional 34.9%, other 25.7%. Fasting: SIMO 1.69 (0.64), p = 0.009; PWG 0.97 (0.37), p = 0.008; SF-12 MCS 0.6 (0.39), p = 0.129; Kessler-10 -0.28 (0.21), p = 0.183; PGIC 0.09 (0.07), p = 0.182. Safe-and-supported mean by context: 3.9, 3.8, 3.4.
Support and safety -0.62 (0.12), p < 0.001; preparation -0.25 (0.07), p = 0.001. Editors' arithmetic: across the 1-4 range (3 points) -1.86 and -0.75 Kessler-10 points on a 10-50 scale.
Authors: many associations were relatively small individually; the links of therapeutic motivation with fear, difficulties and poorer mental health may reflect poorer initial mental health.

Limitations: non-random self-selected sample at risk of bias towards people with positive effects; entirely self-report, several items retrospective (not SF-12 MCS and Kessler-10); no data on mental health before ayahuasca, number of lifetime diagnoses used as an imperfect proxy; no data on the composition, purity or dose of the brew.

anchors.locator: Materials and Methods > Statistical Analysis (3rd paragraph); Discussion (10th paragraph)
anchors.extracted: The GSEM is described as identifying a network of causal relationships, and the conclusion says setting and set appear to have significant effects on acute experiences, integration difficulties and outcomes: causal wording for one cross-sectional self-report survey.

claims.note: Perkins part only. 6,877, -0.29 (editors' 95% CI 0.15 to 0.43 in magnitude, recomputed from SE 0.07: -0.427 to -0.153), -0.13, -0.62 and 'under 2 points' (1.86) all match; ratings averaged 3.4 to 3.9 of 4 by context. The adjustment also included the motivation, ceremony and support variables, not only the covariates listed; the same caveat on model type applies as for cl_aya_ceremony_setting (reading -0.29 as fear-scale points assumes a linear model, which the paper does not state for that outcome).

anchors.locator: Materials and Methods > Study Design (1st paragraph); Discussion (8th paragraph)
anchors.extracted: 6,877 respondents (those who drank with two or fewer groups) from a non-random, self-selected online sample; entirely self-report, retrospective items; authors note possible bias towards people with positive experiences.

anchors.locator: Table 4, row 'Support and safety', columns 'Extreme fear' and 'Integration difficulties'
anchors.extracted: Per point of the 1-4 support-and-safety mean: extreme fear (0-10) -0.29 (SE 0.07), p < 0.001; integration difficulties -0.13 (0.05), p = 0.018; adjusted for age, sex, university education, lifetime diagnoses, times drunk, years since drinking, plus the motivation, ceremony and support variables; n = 6,877 after imputation.
-0.62 (0.12), p < 0.001 on the 10-50 Kessler-10; x 3 points = 1.86 (editors' arithmetic).

anchors.locator: Table 1, 'Safety and support score' items; Table 2, row 'Safe and supported score (1-4)'
anchors.extracted: Item means 3.7-3.8; score by last context 3.9 (church), 3.8 (traditional), 3.4 (other); by region 3.9, 3.7, 3.6.

key_findings.note: The two preparation items sit under 'Additional supports' in Table 1's right-hand column, not under ceremony characteristics; values correct.
Multivariate Models paragraph numbering checked (2nd: ceremony characteristics, intermediate outcomes; 5th: ceremony characteristics, mental health).
University education with fear: B 0.15, SE 0.08 would give p of about 0.06; the printed p = 0.041 is possible only with rounding of B and SE (minor).

reporting_issues.note: Recomputed from the printed ns, means and SDs: F(2, 6,757) = 13.3.

In Table 2 the context panel gives row percentages for the country rows and the region panel gives column percentages for the context rows; both describe the share of mostly-Brazil drinkers who were church members (87.55% vs 87.4%).
The PMC rendering of the companion-paper reference shows DOI and PubMed links, though no journal name or DOI string is printed.

risk_of_bias.note: Very high overall rests on the exposure domain: retrospective, near-ceiling ratings of one's own ceremony whose items overlap the outcomes (feeling safe in the ceremony space vs extreme fear). Domain judgments match my reading.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: causal and 'verify' language for a path model chosen on the same cross-sectional data. Minor: the card's interpretation_gap and analysis fields refer to 'reporting issue 4' for the discussion's departures from the tables, which is index 3 in the 0-based array (the 4th issue).

missed: The paper gives no mean, SD or distribution for the extreme-fear item or the integration-difficulty count (or the other intermediate outcomes), so the coefficients cannot be expressed relative to their spread; only the Kessler-10 scale range allows the editors' whole-range arithmetic.
